name: Atlas: multi-tenant B2B SaaS platform
description: Workflow and approvals SaaS for 5,000 enterprise tenants and 2M monthly users: SSO and SCIM, tenant isolation, audit trail, regional data residency and usage-based billing.
context:
Goal
Re-platform a single-region, single-database workflow product into a multi-tenant B2B SaaS platform that large enterprises can buy: SSO, strict tenant isolation, auditability, regional data residency and usage-based billing. The product is a workflow and approvals engine: forms, routing rules, tasks and integrations.

Scale and targets
- 5,000 tenants today, 15,000 in 24 months. Largest tenant: 120,000 users and 4 million workflow runs a month. 80% of tenants have fewer than 200 users.
- 2 million monthly active users and 20,000 requests/s at peak (weekday 09:00 to 11:00 in each region), about 3x the daily average.
- Availability 99.95% a month for the API and web app. p95 API latency under 250 ms and p99 under 800 ms, not counting customer integrations.
- RPO 5 minutes and RTO 30 minutes for a regional failure.
- Data: 40 TB today, growing about 6 TB a quarter. The audit log grows fastest: 1.2 billion rows a year.

Functional requirements
- Tenants, organisations and workspaces, with roles (admin, builder, approver, viewer) and attribute-based rules such as "approver only when department is Finance".
- Enterprise identity: SAML 2.0 and OIDC single sign-on, SCIM 2.0 provisioning, just-in-time user creation, MFA enforced per tenant.
- Workflow engine: versioned definitions, long-running instances (days to months), timers, retries with backoff, human tasks, webhooks and a public REST and webhook API.
- Immutable audit trail of every change and every read of sensitive data, exportable to the customer's SIEM.
- Usage metering and billing: seats, workflow runs, API calls and storage; monthly invoices built from metered events, with credits and overage.
- Tenant admin console: branding, retention policy, IP allow-list and data export.

Non-functional and compliance
- SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 in place. GDPR, with EU tenant data staying in the EU region. HIPAA-ready for two healthcare tenants (BAA, encryption, access logging).
- Per-tenant encryption keys through KMS, with bring-your-own-key for the top tier. Encryption in transit and at rest.
- Noisy-neighbour protection: per-tenant rate limits, concurrency caps and fair scheduling in the workflow workers.
- Zero-downtime deploys, schema migrations that never lock a big table, feature flags per tenant.

Architecture decisions made, and why
- Pooled model by default: shared services and a shared Postgres cluster, a tenant_id on every row and row-level security. 80% of tenants are small and a database per tenant would cost about 6x as much. The 30 largest tenants get their own siloed databases for isolation and their own maintenance windows.
- Cells: each cell is a full stack (API, workers, database, cache) serving a set of tenants. A thin global routing layer maps tenant to cell and region. The blast radius of a failure is one cell, and new tenants are placed by size and region.
- The workflow engine runs on a durable-execution runtime (Temporal style) instead of a hand-built scheduler. The existing cron-and-queue code is the main source of lost and duplicated runs today.
- Events: a transactional outbox from Postgres to Kafka, with idempotent consumers. Audit and metering read the same event stream, so billing always matches the audit trail.
- Metering pipeline: events to Kafka, stream aggregation per tenant per hour, then a billing ledger table. Invoices come from the ledger, never from raw events.
- Read-heavy admin screens are served from a read replica and a search index (OpenSearch) fed by the event stream.
- The API gateway handles authentication, per-tenant rate limiting (token bucket in Redis) and request IDs. Services trust signed internal tokens only.

Hard problems to work through
- Choosing and enforcing tenant isolation (row-level security, schema or database) and proving it to an auditor.
- Moving 5,000 tenants from the old shared database into cells without downtime: dual writes, backfill, cutover and rollback.
- Fair scheduling across tenants in the workflow workers, and rate limiting at the gateway and inside services.
- Exactly-once effects for webhooks and billing events on top of an at-least-once event stream.
- An audit log of 1.2 billion rows a year: partitioning, tiered storage, fast per-tenant queries and legal-hold deletes.
- Routing tenants to cells with consistent hashing or a directory service, and how to rebalance.

Team and delivery
Four squads (platform, workflow, identity and billing, data) and 28 engineers. Java and Kotlin services, Postgres, Kafka, Redis, Kubernetes on AWS, Terraform. Migration target is 9 months, with tenants moved in waves of 50.

How the labs should help
- System design: interview-grade designs for the cell architecture, the metering pipeline and the audit store, with numbers.
- DSA: the algorithms that show up here: token bucket and sliding-window rate limiters, consistent hashing, LRU caches, interval scheduling for timers, top-k per tenant, graph reachability for permission inheritance.
- Python: small simulators and scripts, such as load models, rate limiter experiments and migration checkers.
- Communication: writing architecture decision records and explaining trade-offs to security reviewers and executives.

name: Helix: real-time payments and fraud platform
description: Payment core for a marketplace and card issuer at 15,000 payments/s peak: event-sourced payment state, a double-entry ledger, acquirer routing, reconciliation and inline fraud scoring.
context:
Goal
Build the payment processing core for a marketplace and card-issuing business: accept, authorise, capture, settle and refund payments across cards, bank transfers and wallets, with real-time fraud decisions and a ledger that finance can trust. It replaces a monolith whose retries sometimes charge a customer twice.

Scale and targets
- 4,000 payments/s on average and 15,000/s at peak (promotions and month end). 1.2 billion payments a year, about 80 billion in volume.
- Authorisation path: p99 under 150 ms inside our systems (card network and issuer time come on top) and 99.99% availability.
- Fraud decision: under 50 ms p99, inline with authorisation. 5% of traffic is also scored asynchronously by a second, slower model.
- Ledger: no lost and no duplicated entries. Every payment reconciles to bank files within one business day.
- Two regions, active-active. RPO of 0 for the ledger and RTO under 5 minutes.

Functional requirements
- Payment lifecycle: create, authorise, capture (partial and multiple), void, refund (partial), chargeback and dispute evidence; 3-D Secure and strong customer authentication.
- Routing: pick the acquirer per payment by cost, success rate, currency and BIN range, with automatic failover and retries on soft declines.
- Idempotency on every write API: client-supplied key, 24 hour window, safe retries.
- Double-entry ledger: every movement is two or more balanced entries, balances are derived and never updated in place, multi-currency with explicit FX entries.
- Payouts to sellers, scheduled and instant, with holds, reserves, fees and tax lines.
- Reconciliation: daily matching against acquirer, bank and card-scheme files, with breaks queued for ops together with a reason.
- Fraud and risk: velocity rules, device and IP signals, ML model scores, a case-management queue, manual review and allow and deny lists. Every decision is explainable and audited.
- Reporting: finance and regulatory reports and an event stream to the warehouse.

Non-functional and compliance
- PCI DSS Level 1: card data lives only in a small, isolated tokenisation vault and everything else sees tokens. PSD2 and SCA in Europe. AML and sanctions screening on payouts.
- Encryption with HSM-backed keys, secret rotation and a full audit of operator access.
- Strict ordering per account and per payment, exactly-once effects on the ledger, at-least-once everywhere else.
- Seven years of retention for ledger and decisions. Right to erasure is handled with tokens and pseudonymisation.

Architecture decisions made, and why
- The payment state machine is the single source of truth per payment, persisted with event sourcing: an append-only event log per payment, projected into read models. It gives a complete audit trail and lets us replay after a bug.
- Outbox pattern for every side effect: a payment event and its outbox row commit in one database transaction and a relay publishes to Kafka. No dual writes.
- Sagas for multi-step flows such as capture then payout, or a refund with fee reversal. They are orchestrated, and every step is idempotent with a compensating action.
- The ledger lives in a strongly consistent relational store (Postgres, serialisable for balance-affecting writes, partitioned by account), not a NoSQL store. Hot accounts such as the platform fee account use sharded sub-accounts and periodic consolidation to avoid a row-lock bottleneck.
- The idempotency store is Redis with a Postgres fallback. The request hash is stored, so a reused key with a different body is rejected.
- Fraud: a feature store (online store for lookups under 10 ms, offline store for training) and a model serving tier behind a rules engine. New models run in shadow mode first, and the system falls back to rules when a model is slow.
- The routing service reads success rates from a sliding-window stream aggregation and applies a circuit breaker per acquirer.
- Multi-region: each payment is homed in one region, deterministically by merchant to keep ordering, with cross-region replication for reads and disaster recovery.

Hard problems to work through
- Exactly-once ledger effects on at-least-once delivery: idempotency keys, deduplication windows, and retries after a timeout when the outcome is unknown.
- Hot-account contention in the ledger, and how to shard it without losing consistency.
- Reconciliation at scale: matching billions of records that carry different identifiers, timing differences and partial settlements.
- Sliding-window success-rate routing and circuit breakers, and the failure modes when an acquirer degrades.
- Real-time fraud features: velocity counters per card, device and IP over several windows, with bounded memory and late events.
- Active-active without double charging, and what happens to in-flight payments in a regional failover.
- Testing: property-based tests for ledger invariants, chaos tests for timeouts, and replay of production traffic.

Team and delivery
Six squads (payments core, ledger, risk, routing, reconciliation, platform) and 45 engineers. Go and Java services, Postgres, Kafka, Redis, Flink for streaming, Kubernetes, Terraform. Rollout by merchant cohort over 12 months, with shadow traffic first.

How the labs should help
- System design: the authorisation path, the ledger and reconciliation, with capacity numbers and failure analysis.
- DSA: sliding windows, heaps and top-k for routing and risk, interval merging for settlements, hashing and Bloom filters for deduplication, graph search for fraud rings, union-find for linked accounts.
- Finance: double-entry accounting, settlement cycles, FX, fees, chargebacks and reconciliation vocabulary, explained for engineers.
- Python: a reconciliation matcher, ledger invariant checks and a simulation of routing under degradation.
- Communication: explaining payment failure modes to non-engineers and writing incident reviews.

name: Compass: enterprise knowledge assistant
description: RAG assistant over 40M documents for 50,000 employees: permission-aware retrieval, citations, evaluation, prompt-injection defences and per-team cost control.
context:
Goal
Give 50,000 employees one assistant that answers questions from the company's own documents, with citations, and never shows anything a person is not allowed to see. It should cut the time people spend searching and reduce repeated questions to the IT, HR and support teams.

Scale and targets
- 50,000 employees in 40 countries. About 12,000 daily active users after the first year and 600 concurrent chats at peak.
- 40 million documents (25 TB) in eight systems: wikis, drive files, tickets, policy libraries, and design docs and READMEs from source repositories. About 400,000 documents change every day.
- Latency: first token under 2 s p95, full answer under 12 s p95, retrieval under 400 ms p95.
- Quality bar before launch: at least 85% of answers on the golden set judged correct and grounded, under 1% of answers with a citation that does not support the claim, and zero permission leaks in red-team tests.
- Cost: under 4 US cents per conversation turn on average, with a monthly budget and alerts per department.

Functional requirements
- Connectors for the eight sources, with incremental sync, deletes and permission sync (users, groups, nested groups and link sharing).
- Permission-aware retrieval: results are filtered by the caller's access at query time and not only at index time. Permission changes reach the index within 5 minutes of the source.
- Chat with citations to the source passages, follow-up questions, an honest "I don't know" when the evidence is weak, and links to open the source.
- Hybrid search (keyword plus vector) with re-ranking, query rewriting for follow-ups, and four languages: English, German, Spanish and Japanese.
- Actions with approval: create a ticket, draft an email, fill a form. Every action needs an explicit confirmation from the user.
- Feedback (thumbs and corrections), analytics for content owners ("what people ask and do not find") and admin controls per department.

Non-functional, safety and governance
- Data stays in our cloud tenant. No employee data is used to train external models, and vendor contracts require zero retention.
- PII and secrets detection on ingestion and on output, with redaction policies per department. Retention follows the source system.
- Defences against prompt injection from documents (documents are untrusted input), against jailbreaks, and against data exfiltration through tool calls. Only allow-listed tools can run.
- A full audit log of questions, retrieved passages, model versions and answers, with restricted access and 90 days of retention.
- A model gateway with provider fallback, rate limits, caching and budgets per team.

Architecture decisions made, and why
- Ingestion pipeline: connector, normaliser, structure-aware chunker (300 to 500 tokens, with titles and headings carried into each chunk), embedding, then a vector index and a keyword index. Changes flow through a queue, so an update only re-embeds the chunks that changed.
- Permissions are stored as access-control lists per document, with expanded group memberships cached and refreshed incrementally. The filter is applied inside the vector search (pre-filter), with a post-check before generation as a second layer.
- Retrieval: hybrid search, reciprocal-rank fusion, a cross-encoder re-rank of the top 50 down to the top 8, and query rewriting that uses the conversation history. A small router chooses between searching, answering directly and asking a clarifying question.
- Generation: a grounded prompt with numbered passages and a strict citation format, plus a verifier step that checks each claim against its cited passage. Weak evidence leads to an abstention.
- Evaluation is a product feature: a golden set of 1,500 questions by department, an automatic regression run on every prompt, model, chunking or index change, an LLM judge calibrated against human labels, and online metrics from feedback.
- Serving: a stateless chat service with streaming responses, a semantic cache for common questions (only for content visible to everyone) and per-team concurrency limits.
- Observability: traces from the query to the retrieved chunks to the model call, with token and cost accounting per request.

Hard problems to work through
- Permission-aware retrieval across 40 million documents: pre-filter versus post-filter, group explosion, and keeping access lists fresh.
- Chunking and metadata for different document types (tables, slides, code, tickets) and how they change recall.
- Evaluating retrieval and answers: recall at k, MRR, groundedness and citation precision, how to design the golden set and how to catch regressions.
- Prompt-injection and exfiltration defences in a system that reads untrusted documents and can take actions.
- Controlling cost and latency: caching, routing between small and large models, and context budgeting.
- Index design: sharding, incremental updates, and re-indexing with a new embedding model without downtime.
- Failure modes: a stale index, connector outages, confident but wrong answers, and how the interface shows uncertainty.

Team and delivery
Squads for connectors, retrieval, assistant experience, evaluation and platform security: 22 engineers and 3 applied scientists. Python services, Postgres, an OpenSearch and vector index, a queue, Kubernetes, and a model gateway in front of two hosted model providers and one self-hosted open model. Pilot with 2,000 users in 3 months and the whole company in 9.

How the labs should help
- GenAI and AI lab: RAG, hybrid search, re-ranking, evaluation, guardrails and agents, explained against this system.
- System design: the ingestion pipeline, the permission filter and the serving path, with numbers.
- DSA: inverted indexes, approximate nearest-neighbour search, top-k heaps, tries for query suggestions, LRU and LFU caches, Bloom filters for deduplication, graph traversal for nested groups.
- Python: ingestion and evaluation scripts, a small retrieval benchmark and ACL expansion code.
- Communication: briefing security, legal and executives on risk, and writing the launch criteria.
